seg_p0036_s0001: Hence Arnobius: "So swiftly does his word run that, although for so many thousands of years God was known in Judaea alone, now, within a few years, it is hidden neither from the Indians themselves in the east nor from the Britons themselves in the west.
seg_p0036_s0002: Everywhere his word has run swiftly." Gildas, however, indicates that Christ first granted the rays of his truth to Britain between this last period of Tiberius Caesar — when the light of the Gospel began to be spread throughout the whole world — and the campaign waged by the Romans against the Britons (after that very great disaster suffered at the hands of queen Boadicia, whom he calls "the treacherous Lioness"), of which he had just been speaking; that is, between the year 36 of our common Christian era and the year 61 (in which the province was once again recovered by Suetonius Paulinus, with eighty thousand of the Britons slain).
seg_p0036_s0003: Hence Theodoret too, in the ninth book of the Ἑλλήνων παθημάτων θεραπευτικῆς ["The Cure of the Greek Maladies"], numbers the Britons among the peoples converted to the faith by the ministry of the apostles: Οἱ δὲ ἡμέτεροι ἁλιεῖς, καὶ οἱ τελώναι, καὶ ὁ σκυτοτόμος ἅπασιν ἀνθρώποις τοὺς εὐαγγελικοὺς προσενηνόχασι νόμους· καὶ οὐ μόνον Ῥωμαίους καὶ ὑπὸ τούτοις τελοῦντας, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ Σκυθικὰ καὶ τὰ Σαυροματικὰ ἔθνη, καὶ Ἰνδοὺς καὶ Αἰθίοπας, καὶ Πέρσας καὶ Σῆρας, καὶ Ὑρκανοὺς, καὶ Βακτριανοὺς, καὶ Βρεττανοὺς, καὶ Κίμβρους, καὶ Γερμανοὺς, καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς πᾶν ἔθνος καὶ γένος ἀνθρώπων, δέξασθαι τοῦ σταυρωθέντος τοὺς νόμους ἀνέπεισαν [Our own fishermen and tax-collectors, he says, and that cobbler of ours, have brought the teachings of the Gospel to all men; and they have persuaded not only the Romans and those who live under their rule, but also the Scythian and Sarmatian peoples, the Indians and Ethiopians, the Persians and Seres, the Hyrcanians and Bactrians, the Britons and the Cimbri and the Germans, and, to say it once for all, every nation and race of men, to accept the teachings of the Crucified One]. But as to which member of that company of apostles came to our British isles, the authors are not all of one opinion.
seg_p0036_s0004: Some report — from the book on the sufferings of the martyrs by Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, written in Arabic — that St. James the son of Zebedee, the brother of John, went away into the west and performed many miracles in those regions. Isidore too, in his book on the fathers of both Testaments, records that the same man "preached the Gospel to the peoples of Spain and of the western regions, and poured the light of his preaching into the setting of the world"; and following him, Freculf of Lisieux. The author of the chronicle that circulates under the name of Maximus, bishop of Saragossa, likewise asserts that he "preached on the western shores before all the other apostles." That he preached to the Britons is affirmed by the man who has put on the mask of Flavius Lucius Dexter, and that he preached to the Irish by Vincent of Beauvais. For the former says, in his chronicle, at the year of Christ 41: "On his return James visited Gaul, and the Britains, and the towns of the Veneti, where he preaches; and he returns to Jerusalem to consult the blessed Virgin and Peter on matters of the gravest importance." The latter, in his "Speculum Historiale" (and cited also at the Council of Basel by Alfonso García de Santa María, ambassador of the king of Castile), writes thus: "While the apostles were going to the various regions of the world, James, by the will of God, having landed on the shores of Ireland, fearlessly preached the word of God, where he is said to have chosen seven disciples: namely Torquatus, Secundus, Indaletius, Tisephon, Euphrasius, Caecilius, and Hesychius, that by their fellowship he might root out the tares and commit the seeds of the word of God to the dry and long-barren earth. And when his last day drew near, he went on with them to Jerusalem, and there underwent martyrdom."
